title: Former Envoy Warns Trump's Green Card Curbs May Rupture India-US Ties
excerpt: Former Indian ambassador Javed Ashraf told NDTV that US restrictions on students, H-1B workers and green-card applicants are eroding the "social bridge" between the two countries, days after Washington froze PERM applications for eight major firms including Microsoft, Infosys and TCS.
body:
• Former Indian ambassador Javed Ashraf told NDTV that repeated US restrictions on students, H-1B holders and green-card applicants are "rupturing the social bridge" that anchors the India-US partnership.
  • On October 8, the Trump administration froze new and pending PERM green-card applications for eight companies — Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini — citing alleged fraud and abuse.
  • India's foreign ministry pushed back, saying the steps "do not advance both countries' shared ambitions" and calling descriptions of Indian professionals "unwarranted."
  • What it means for you: the freeze affects only employer-sponsored PERM cases at the eight named companies; existing H-1B status is untouched, pending cases are frozen rather than cancelled, and employer-independent routes such as EB-1A and EB-2 National Interest Waiver remain open. Workers nearing the six-year H-1B limit at the suspended firms face the most immediate risk — and no end date for the freeze has been announced.

Ashraf: Washington Is Rupturing the Bridge, Layer by Layer

Speaking to NDTV on October 10, former Indian ambassador Javed Ashraf described the Indian diaspora in the United States as a "foundational pillar" of the bilateral relationship — the social bridge that connected India's educated, aspirational middle class to American innovation and carried a window on India's potential to the world.

That bridge, he warned, is now being ruptured "at every level — student level, H-1B level, green card level, professional and every level" — and the damage will show in the relationship in the coming years.

"You rupture that social bridge at every level … and you can see the impact on the relationship in the coming years."

— Javed Ashraf, former Indian ambassador, to NDTV

Ashraf said India's restraint in the face of Washington's pressure campaign may have been "misunderstood" — read as permission to keep escalating "with no particular cost to them or to the relationship." He added that the Trump administration is "in no mood to relent," suggesting the push is driven by perceived grievances, the desire to extract concessions, and, increasingly, populist signaling ahead of the US midterm elections.

Context & Background: The October 8 PERM Freeze

Ashraf's warning landed two days after a dramatic White House announcement. On October 8, Vice President JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling told reporters the Department of Labor would stop accepting new Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) applications — and stop processing pending ones — involving eight employers: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. Meta, Amazon and Google were notably not on the list.

PERM, in place since 2005, is the first mandatory step when a US employer sponsors an H-1B worker for an employment-based green card. The Labor Department must certify that no qualified American workers are available for the job and that the foreign hire will not depress wages or conditions. Without it, hundreds of thousands of IT workers who start on H-1B visas lose their main route to permanent residency.

The administration's case rests on allegations of fraud. Vance singled out Microsoft, claiming the company laid off roughly 6,000 American employees over the past year while securing 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards — arguing the pattern showed foreign "indentured servants" replacing American workers. Microsoft countered that 80 percent of its H-1B filings last fiscal year were extensions or status changes for existing employees, not new arrivals, and that its H-1B wages rank among the highest of all filings.

The freeze follows the administration's earlier move to impose a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions — a fee currently blocked by federal court orders, according to Reuters. The PERM action is separate: existing H-1B visas remain valid, and H-1B applications continue under separate rules.

Impact & Analysis: A Diplomatic Rebuke From Delhi

India's Ministry of External Affairs issued a sharp response, saying: "The steps do not advance both countries' shared ambitions." The ministry added that Vance's descriptions were "unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem."

The diplomatic exchange marks a hardening tone. Immigration policy has become a lever in the broader relationship — one that now touches not just workers but the students, engineers and professionals Ashraf described as the relationship's connective tissue.

Policy analysts warn the curbs could backfire on American competitiveness. Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab and Colgate University researchers note that permanent residency is the primary reason talented foreign workers choose to stay — and that shutting the route does not keep talent home so much as push it to compete with the US from abroad.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, this is the third pressure point in a single season: student visas under scrutiny, a $100,000 H-1B fee hanging in court limbo, and now the green-card pipeline frozen for employees of the very firms — Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL, Cognizant — that employ the largest numbers of Indian H-1B workers. Immigration lawyers warn that workers who followed every rule and have spent years on temporary status are now watching their green-card cases stall over a dispute they had no part in — a particular threat to those approaching the six-year H-1B ceiling, when legal work status can lapse if no sponsorship path remains.

The cultural fallout may outlast any single freeze. Ashraf's "social bridge" argument is that the diaspora's power flowed from two-way movement — students becoming founders, engineers becoming bridges — and that curbing each layer progressively narrows the aperture through which the next generation imagines an American future.

What's Next

No timeline has been given for lifting the PERM suspensions, which cover pending cases as well as new filings. Microsoft has said it looks forward to providing the administration with more information — a response that came hours before President Trump awarded CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House, an irony not lost on observers.

The larger question is whether the freeze expands beyond the eight named companies or is followed by further curbs — and whether New Delhi's unusually blunt pushback signals a new phase in which immigration policy becomes an explicit irritant in bilateral ties. For Indian workers and students planning their futures, the watchpoint is the next announcement from the Labor Department and the courts' handling of the $100,000 H-1B fee — both will shape the shape of the pipeline for years.
